To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
terrain wetness and proximity to roads are the most important factors in the regeneration of legacy seismic disturbances in the boreal forest.
the probability of regeneration of trees and shrub on legacy seismic lines was inversely related (1) to terrain wetness (2) line width (3) proximity to roads (4) and the lowland (fen) ecosites.
terrain wetness and proximity to roads were key determinants of regeneration patterns of trees on seismic lines in the boreal forest of Alberta, Canada.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regeneration of forest vegetation in a boreal landscape impacted by seismic lines.
the effects of linear disturbances on forest vegetation and the potential for recovery of these disturbances.
the long term effects of linear disturbance on forest regeneration and the potential for recovery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the natural regeneration of vegetation on legacy seismic line disturbance is highly variable, and that the probability of regeneration is influenced by local and landscape scale factors, with the strongest influence from terrain wetness and ecosite.
the legacy of linear disturbances in the boreal forest of Alberta will persist for many decades, with a high likelihood of remaining a significant source of habitat fragmentation.
the legacy seismic lines in the boreal forest of Alberta’s oil sands are unlikely to be fully re-forested in the foreseeable future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
natural regeneration of vegetation on legacy seismic line disturbances in this region is slow, but not impossible, and is affected by local and landscape-scale factors.
the wettest sites are least likely to recover and that the legacy of linear disturbances will be long lasting.
the legacy of seismic lines in this landscape will persist for at least the next 50 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
natural regeneration is not always a reliable process for restoring forest vegetation on linear disturbances in wet habitats.
the wetter and lower lying areas of the landscape will not recover to forest cover in the next 50 years.
the legacy seismic line disturbances will persist as linear habitat features for at least another 50 years, and likely much longer, unless they are mitigated by restoration efforts.
